papers.title: Free-standing two-dimensional metal oxides at the single-atomic-layer limit
papers.authors: Meng Gao, Deping Guo, Ang Li, Renhong Wang, Zhitong Jin, Chun Huang, Yixiang Lu, Yuhao Pan, Jiuxiang Dai, Panqi Huang, Kangjie Liu, Cong Wang, Lihong Bao, Lin Zhou, Jingsi Qiao, Wei Ji, Stephen J. Pennycook, Hong-Jun Gao, Wu Zhou
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional metal oxides offer a versatile platform for exploring quantum phenomena and enable functionalities beyond those of their bulk counterparts. Despite advances in synthesizing ultrathin and free-standing oxides, controlled fabrication at the single-atomic-layer limit has remained a formidable challenge. Here we report the controlled fabrication of diverse free-standing two-dimensional metal oxides (MO), including CrO, ErO and BiO, down to the single-atomic-layer limit via electron-beam-induced dehalogenation of layered metal oxyhalides (MOX). Using monolayer CrO as a representative system, which features a single-atomic-layer square lattice, we obtain free-standing single-crystalline domains exceeding 104 nm2 and demonstrate controllable patterning at the micrometre scale. Density functional theory confirms both the thermodynamic and kinetic stability of free-standing monolayer CrO, predicting a Néel antiferromagnetic order below 230 K. Combined experimental and theoretical analysis reveals that ionization-driven halogen selective removal and lattice relaxation underpin the CrOCl-to-CrO transformation, a conversion mechanism potentially extendable to other metal oxyhalides. This approach further enables the fabrication of MOX–MO lateral heterostructures as well as aligned and twisted metal oxide bilayers, which exhibit pronounced excitonic responses with an unusually large exciton binding energy. Our work opens opportunities for two-dimensional metal oxide monolayers, heterostructures and moiré superlattices, and for exploring emergent excitonic phenomena in low-dimensional oxides. The electron-beam-assisted subtraction method enables the controllable fabrication of free-standing metal oxide monolayers, along with lateral heterostructures and twisted bilayers, expanding the material space of 2D quantum systems.
papers.summary_en: The authors report controlled fabrication of free-standing CrO, ErO and BiO metal-oxide layers down to the single-atomic-layer limit by electron-beam-induced dehalogenation of layered metal oxyhalides. The work also demonstrates patterning, lateral heterostructures and aligned or twisted oxide bilayers.

papers.title: Probing spin order via magnon transmission across quantum Hall ferromagnet heterojunctions
papers.authors: Seung Hwan Lee, Shaowen Chen, Andrew T. Pierce, Patrick R. Forrester, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Amir Yacoby
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional material platforms host a remarkable array of exotic correlated phases. Probing magnetic order in these systems is essential for understanding their underlying physics, yet dilute spin densities render conventional magnetic probes ineffective. Spin waves, or magnons, in quantum Hall ferromagnets (QHFM) have proven effective for probing the magnetic order in various symmetry-broken quantum Hall (QH) phases in graphene systems, but previous works have been limited to homojunction configurations within a single material. Here, we demonstrate magnon transmission across a monolayer-bilayer graphene quantum Hall ferromagnet heterojunction—the first magnon transmission across quantum Hall ferromagnet heterojunctions, using one material as a magnon source to probe magnetic order in a distinct material. Generating magnons in monolayer graphene (MLG) at νMLG = 1, we detect their transmission through bilayer graphene (BLG) via nonlocal voltage measurements, revealing spin order in BLG symmetry-broken quantum Hall states. The transmission exhibits hallmark magnon signatures: a sharp onset at the Zeeman energy and systematic variation with Landau level filling, including suppression at νBLG = 4 and 8 where spin polarization vanishes. Our findings establish heterojunction magnon transmission as a powerful, modular probe of magnetic order, opening new avenues for investigating exotic quantum states across the rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional materials. Magnons in quantum Hall ferromagnets can be used as a very sensitive probe of magnetic order. Thus far, this technique has only been applied to single material systems. Here, Lee et al extend this to a heterostructure, using magnons generated in a monolayer of graphene to detect spin order in bilayer graphene.
papers.summary_en: The authors demonstrate magnon transmission across a monolayer–bilayer graphene quantum Hall ferromagnet heterojunction, extending this probe beyond single-material systems. Magnons generated in monolayer graphene reveal spin order in symmetry-broken quantum Hall states of bilayer graphene.

papers.title: Imaging hot-electron Thomson cooling beyond the Boltzmann–Onsager framework
papers.authors: Xinrong Zuo, Guokang Zhang, Weikang Lu, Anish Das, Guijian Pang, Ziyi Xu, Ludi Qin, Chengfeng Ding, Hongtao Xu, Siyu Duan, Ziteng Zhang, Pingping Chen, Wu Li, Zhenghua An
papers.abstract: Classical Thomson cooling, constrained by lattice-dominated heat dissipation and the weak entropy variation of charge carriers under thermal equilibrium, remains inefficient within the Boltzmann–Onsager framework. Driving electrons far from equilibrium broadens their energy spectrum and smears the Fermi edge, and this amplifies the temperature dependence of the electronic entropy. However, the hot-electron thermoelectric response beyond the classical thermal equilibrium limit has remained unexplored due to the lack of direct access to hot-electron dynamics. Here we image spatial distributions of electron and lattice temperatures together with the corresponding thermoelectric signals in HgTe and HgCdTe nanoconstrictions using coupled scanning-probe techniques. In HgTe, weak electron–phonon coupling allows hot electrons to remain far from thermal equilibrium with the lattice, and this generates large electron temperature gradients and a pronounced Thomson compensation effect. In HgCdTe the response shifts towards lattice-mediated heat redistribution due to the suppressed non-equilibrium state. These observations reveal a pronounced departure from the conventional near-equilibrium Boltzmann–Onsager expectations in high-field thermoelectricity, identify the Thomson effect as a key channel of non-equilibrium energy dissipation and establish a platform for exploring non-equilibrium thermoelectric phenomena in nanoscale conductors. Classical Thomson cooling is inefficient. Now non-equilibrium energy dissipation with a breakdown of the Boltzmann–Onsager limit is demonstrated by imaging hot electrons in HgTe and HgCdTe quantum wells.
papers.summary_en: The authors image electron and lattice temperatures and thermoelectric signals in HgTe and HgCdTe nanoconstrictions, revealing hot-electron Thomson cooling beyond near-equilibrium Boltzmann–Onsager expectations. The response differs between the materials in relation to how strongly hot electrons remain out of equilibrium with the lattice.

papers.summary_zh: 作者对 HgTe 和 HgCdTe 纳米收缩结构中的电子温度、晶格温度及热电信号进行成像，揭示了超出近似平衡玻尔兹曼—昂萨格预期的热电子汤姆孙冷却。两种材料的响应有所不同，这与热电子偏离晶格平衡的程度有关。
papers.method_en: The study uses coupled scanning-probe techniques to image spatial distributions of electron and lattice temperatures alongside thermoelectric signals in HgTe and HgCdTe nanoconstrictions. Comparing the two materials enables the authors to examine responses with different degrees of non-equilibrium between electrons and the lattice.

papers.result_en: In HgTe, weak electron–phonon coupling allows hot electrons to remain far from equilibrium with the lattice. This is accompanied by large electron-temperature gradients and a pronounced Thomson compensation effect. In HgCdTe, the non-equilibrium state is suppressed and the response shifts towards lattice-mediated heat redistribution. The observations reveal a departure from conventional near-equilibrium Boltzmann–Onsager expectations and identify the Thomson effect as a channel of non-equilibrium energy dissipation.

papers.future_en: The authors identify nanoscale conductors as a platform for exploring non-equilibrium thermoelectric phenomena. Further work can use spatially resolved electron and lattice temperatures to investigate such responses beyond the near-equilibrium regime.
papers.future_zh: 作者指出，纳米尺度导体可作为探索非平衡热电现象的平台。后续研究可利用电子与晶格温度的空间分辨测量，探究近似平衡区间之外的此类响应。
